questions.title: A fractional shift
questions.prompt_html: Write \(x^2+5x-2\) in completed-square form.
questions.hint_html: Keep the half-coefficient as an exact fraction.
questions.solution_html:
1. Use \(\left(x+\frac52\right)^2\), which adds \(\frac{25}{4}\).
  2. Subtract \(\frac{25}{4}\) and then 2: \(-\frac{25}{4}-2=-\frac{33}{4}\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: Write \(2=8/4\) before combining constants.

questions.title: Keep the outside coefficient
questions.prompt_html: Write \(3x^2-12x+17\) in completed-square form.
questions.hint_html: The correction inside the bracket is also multiplied by 3.
questions.solution_html:
1. Factor 3 from the first two terms: \(3(x^2-4x)+17\).
  2. \(3[(x-2)^2-4]+17=3(x-2)^2+5\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: You subtracted 4 rather than 12 from the original constant.

questions.title: A fractional leading coefficient
questions.prompt_html: Find the coordinates of the vertex of \(y=\frac12x^2-3x+8\) by completing the square.
questions.hint_html: First factor \(\frac12\) from the terms containing x.
questions.solution_html:
1. \(y=\frac12(x^2-6x)+8=\frac12(x-3)^2+\frac72\).
  2. The square vanishes at \(x=3\), so the vertex is \((3,\frac72)\).

marking_criteria.description_html: The square vanishes at \(x=3\), so the vertex is \((3,\frac72)\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: The linear coefficient inside the bracket is \(-6\), not \(-3\).
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Check that \(\frac12(-6x)=-3x\).

questions.title: A positive quadratic
questions.prompt_html: Find the least value of \(4x^2+4x+7\), and explain why the expression is positive for every real \(x\). Sketch the graph, labelling its vertex and y-intercept.
questions.hint_html: Give a lower bound from the completed-square form.
questions.answer_html: Least value \(6\), at \(x=-\frac12\); it is always positive. Sketch an upward-opening parabola with vertex \((-\frac12,6)\), y-intercept \((0,7)\), and no x-intercepts.
questions.solution_html:
1. \(4x^2+4x+7=4(x+\frac12)^2+6\).
  2. The square is nonnegative, so the expression is at least 6; equality occurs at \(x=-\frac12\).
  3. The graph opens upwards, has vertex \((-\frac12,6)\), passes through \((0,7)\), and stays above the x-axis.

marking_criteria.description_html: The square is nonnegative, so the expression is at least 6; equality occurs at \(x=-\frac12\).
Sketch an upward-opening curve with correctly labelled vertex and y-intercept, entirely above the x-axis.

misconceptions.likely_wrong_answer_html: It is positive because the coefficient of x² is positive.
misconceptions.feedback_html: An upward-opening parabola can still cross the x-axis.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Use the actual minimum, 6.

questions.title: Vertex inside a closed domain
questions.prompt_html: Find the range of \(f(x)=2(x-3)^2-5\) for \(-1\le x\le4\).
questions.hint_html: Check the vertex and both endpoints.
questions.solution_html:
1. The vertex at \(x=3\) is included, giving the minimum \(-5\).
  2. Endpoint values are \(f(-1)=27\) and \(f(4)=-3\).
  3. The maximum is 27 and both extrema are attained, so the range is \([-5,27]\).

marking_criteria.description_html: The vertex at \(x=3\) is included, giving the minimum \(-5\).
The maximum is 27 and both extrema are attained, so the range is \([-5,27]\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: The minimum occurs at an interior point, not at an endpoint.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Check whether \(x=3\) belongs to the domain.

questions.title: Vertex outside the domain
questions.prompt_html: Find the range of \(g(x)=-(x+2)^2+9\) for \(0\le x\le3\).
questions.hint_html: A vertex outside the domain does not provide an attained extreme value.
questions.solution_html:
1. The vertex \(x=-2\) is outside the domain; \((x+2)^2\) increases on this interval.
  2. \(g(0)=5\) and \(g(3)=-16\).
  3. Thus the attained range is \([-16,5]\), not a range ending at 9.

marking_criteria.description_html: The vertex \(x=-2\) is outside the domain; \((x+2)^2\) increases on this interval.
Thus the attained range is \([-16,5]\), not a range ending at 9.

misconceptions.feedback_html: The value 9 requires \(x=-2\), which is not allowed.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Evaluate the function at the allowed endpoints.

questions.title: Reconstruct a quadratic
questions.prompt_html: A quadratic has vertex \((-3,-4)\) and passes through \((1,28)\). Find its equation in completed-square and expanded forms.
questions.hint_html: Start with the vertex form, leaving the scale factor unknown.
questions.solution_html:
1. The vertex gives \(y=a(x+3)^2-4\).
  2. Using \((1,28)\): \(28=16a-4\), so \(a=2\).
  3. Expand to obtain \(y=2x^2+12x+14\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: The vertex alone does not determine the leading coefficient.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Use the additional point to determine \(a\).

questions.title: Strict positivity for all x
questions.prompt_html: Find all real \(k\) for which \(x^2-6x+k\gt 0\) for every real \(x\).
questions.hint_html: Distinguish positive from nonnegative.
questions.solution_html:
1. \(x^2-6x+k=(x-3)^2+k-9\).
  2. The minimum is \(k-9\); strict positivity requires \(k-9\gt 0\), so \(k\gt 9\).

marking_criteria.description_html: The minimum is \(k-9\); strict positivity requires \(k-9\gt 0\), so \(k\gt 9\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: At \(k=9,x=3\), the expression equals zero.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Test the boundary parameter in the original inequality.

questions.title: Count roots on a restricted domain
questions.prompt_html: For \(0\le x\le4\), let \(f(x)=2(x-1)^2+3\). Find all \(k\) for which \(f(x)=k\) has exactly two distinct solutions in this domain.
questions.hint_html: Two algebraic roots are not necessarily two roots in the stated domain.
questions.solution_html:
1. For two distinct real roots, write \(x=1\pm r\), with \(r=\sqrt{(k-3)/2}\gt 0\).
  2. Both roots belong to \([0,4]\) only if \(1-r\ge0\), hence \(r\le1\); this also ensures \(1+r\le4\).
  3. Thus \(0\lt (k-3)/2\le1\), giving \(3\lt k\le5\). At \(k=5\) the two roots are 0 and 2.

marking_criteria.description_html: For two distinct real roots, write \(x=1\pm r\), with \(r=\sqrt{(k-3)/2}\gt 0\).
Both roots belong to \([0,4]\) only if \(1-r\ge0\), hence \(r\le1\); this also ensures \(1+r\le4\).
Thus \(0\lt (k-3)/2\le1\), giving \(3\lt k\le5\). At \(k=5\) the two roots are 0 and 2.

misconceptions.feedback_html: Above height 5, the left-hand root is negative and leaves the allowed domain.

questions.title: Build a graph from its vertex
questions.stem_html: The graph of a quadratic function \(f\) has vertex \((2,-7)\) and passes through \((0,5)\).

parts.hint_html: The vertex determines the shift and constant, but not the scale.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use vertex form with an unknown scale factor.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the exact x-intercepts of the graph.
parts.label: b

parts.solution_html:
1. \(3(x-2)^2-7\le5\) gives \((x-2)^2\le4\).
  2. Hence \(0\le x\le4\).
  3. Intersect with the given domain to obtain \([1,4]\).
parts.hint_html: Apply the domain after solving the inequality.

misconceptions.feedback_html: The question also restricts x to [1,6].
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Take the overlap.

parts.label: c

questions.prompt_html:
The graph of a quadratic function \(f\) has vertex \((2,-7)\) and passes through \((0,5)\).

  1. Find \(f(x)\) in completed-square form.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact x-intercepts of the graph.

    [2]

  3. Find all \(x\) in \([1,6]\) for which \(f(x)\le5\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

  1. Write \(f(x)=a(x-2)^2-7\).
  2. \(5=4a-7\) gives \(a=3\).

(b)

  1. \(3(x-2)^2=7\).
  2. \(x=2\pm\sqrt{7/3}=2\pm\sqrt{21}/3\).

(c)

  1. \(3(x-2)^2-7\le5\) gives \((x-2)^2\le4\).
  2. Hence \(0\le x\le4\).
  3. Intersect with the given domain to obtain \([1,4]\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) The vertex determines the shift and constant, but not the scale.

(b) Set the y-value equal to zero.

(c) Apply the domain after solving the inequality.

misconceptions.feedback_html: The question also restricts x to [1,6].
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Take the overlap.

questions.title: A restricted downward parabola

parts.hint_html: Be careful with the negative outside coefficient.

marking_criteria.description_html: Factor the leading coefficient from the first two terms.

parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the range of \(h\) on this domain.
parts.solution_html:
1. The included vertex gives maximum 9 at x=3.
  2. \(h(0)=-9\), \(h(4)=7\); hence the minimum on the domain is -9.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all real \(t\) for which \(h(x)=t\) has exactly one solution in \([0,4]\).
parts.solution_html:
1. For levels from -9 up to but not including 7, only the increasing branch inside the domain is met.
  2. At t=7 there are two solutions, x=2 and x=4; for \(7\lt t\lt 9\) there are also two.
  3. At t=9 only the vertex x=3 remains. Levels outside [-9,9] give no solutions.
parts.hint_html: Compare the vertex height with the heights at both endpoints.

marking_criteria.description_html: Justify the exclusion of 7 and the boundary cases.

misconceptions.feedback_html: At t=7 both x=2 and x=4 are allowed.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Test the boundary level rather than guessing its inclusion.

parts.label: c

questions.prompt_html:
Let \(h(x)=-2x^2+12x-9\), with domain \(0\le x\le4\).

  1. Write \(h(x)\) in completed-square form.

    [3]

  2. Find the range of \(h\) on this domain.

    [2]

  3. Find all real \(t\) for which \(h(x)=t\) has exactly one solution in \([0,4]\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

  1. \(h(x)=-2(x^2-6x)-9\).
  2. \(h(x)=-2[(x-3)^2-9]-9=-2(x-3)^2+9\).

(b)

  1. The included vertex gives maximum 9 at x=3.
  2. \(h(0)=-9\), \(h(4)=7\); hence the minimum on the domain is -9.

(c)

  1. For levels from -9 up to but not including 7, only the increasing branch inside the domain is met.
  2. At t=7 there are two solutions, x=2 and x=4; for \(7\lt t\lt 9\) there are also two.
  3. At t=9 only the vertex x=3 remains. Levels outside [-9,9] give no solutions.
questions.hint_html:
(a) Be careful with the negative outside coefficient.

(b) Check both endpoints and the vertex.

(c) Compare the vertex height with the heights at both endpoints.

misconceptions.feedback_html: At t=7 both x=2 and x=4 are allowed.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Test the boundary level rather than guessing its inclusion.

questions.title: A minimum that depends on a parameter

parts.solution_html:
1. Factor 2 from the x-terms and use the shift \(x-(k+1)\).
  2. \(2[x-(k+1)]^2-2(k+1)^2+2k^2+3=2(x-k-1)^2+1-4k\).
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all \(k\) such that \(f_k(x)\gt 0\) for every real \(x\).
parts.hint_html: For every x, the lowest value must still be positive.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the minimum to express strict positivity.

parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: At the boundary value \(k=\frac14\), solve \(f_k(x)=0\) and describe the root.
parts.solution_html:
1. At k=1/4, \(f_k(x)=2(x-5/4)^2\).
  2. The equation has the repeated root x=5/4.
parts.hint_html: The minimum becomes zero at this boundary.

marking_criteria.description_html: Substitute the boundary into the completed-square form.

parts.label: c

questions.prompt_html:
For real \(k\), let \(f_k(x)=2x^2-4(k+1)x+2k^2+3\).

  1. Write \(f_k(x)\) in completed-square form.

    [3]

  2. Find all \(k\) such that \(f_k(x)\gt 0\) for every real \(x\).

    [2]

  3. At the boundary value \(k=\frac14\), solve \(f_k(x)=0\) and describe the root.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

  1. Factor 2 from the x-terms and use the shift \(x-(k+1)\).
  2. \(2[x-(k+1)]^2-2(k+1)^2+2k^2+3=2(x-k-1)^2+1-4k\).

(b)

  1. The minimum is \(1-4k\), attained at \(x=k+1\).
  2. Require \(1-4k\gt 0\), so \(k\lt 1/4\).

(c)

  1. At k=1/4, \(f_k(x)=2(x-5/4)^2\).
  2. The equation has the repeated root x=5/4.
questions.hint_html:
(a) Expand \((k+1)^2\) carefully.

(b) For every x, the lowest value must still be positive.

(c) The minimum becomes zero at this boundary.

questions.title: Two quadratics with the same minimum

parts.prompt_html: Find the minimum value of \(g_h\) in terms of \(h\), and state where it occurs.
parts.solution_html:
1. \(g_h(x)=(x-h)^2+4+h-h^2\).
  2. The square is zero at x=h, which gives the minimum.
parts.hint_html: Keep h as a parameter while completing the square.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find all \(h\) for which this minimum equals 2.
parts.hint_html: The condition on a minimum can itself be a quadratic equation.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: For each value of \(h\) from part (b), solve \(g_h(x)=6\).
parts.hint_html: Use the two completed-square forms, not a new expansion.

misconceptions.feedback_html: Each pair belongs to a different quadratic.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Label each answer by its parameter value.

parts.label: c

questions.prompt_html:
For a real parameter \(h\), let \(g_h(x)=x^2-2hx+h+4\).

  1. Find the minimum value of \(g_h\) in terms of \(h\), and state where it occurs.

    [3]

  2. Find all \(h\) for which this minimum equals 2.

    [3]

  3. For each value of \(h\) from part (b), solve \(g_h(x)=6\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

  1. \(g_h(x)=(x-h)^2+4+h-h^2\).
  2. The square is zero at x=h, which gives the minimum.

(b)

  1. \(4+h-h^2=2\) gives \(h^2-h-2=0\).
  2. \((h-2)(h+1)=0\), so h=2 or -1.

(c)

  1. For h=2, \((x-2)^2+2=6\), so x=0 or 4.
  2. For h=-1, \((x+1)^2+2=6\), so x=-3 or 1.
questions.hint_html:
(a) Keep h as a parameter while completing the square.

(b) The condition on a minimum can itself be a quadratic equation.

(c) Use the two completed-square forms, not a new expansion.

misconceptions.feedback_html: Each pair belongs to a different quadratic.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Label each answer by its parameter value.
